UK PARROT BUYING ENQUIRIES

African grey parrots for UK homes

Enquiries can be made about African Grey Parrots, including the Congo and Timneh types, but that does not confirm a particular species, bird or service is currently available. Use the conversation to establish the identity and individual needs of the bird being discussed, then decide whether they fit your home.

Available by enquiry

African Grey Parrots are available through Crownwing. Individual birds change regularly. Contact us for current birds, photographs and prices.

Species photographs are not individual stock listings.

Start with the individual bird

Ask whether the enquiry concerns a Congo African grey or a Timneh, and what information supports that identification. Request the bird's known age or best available age information, sex if known, and a clear description of its current routine. If any detail is uncertain, ask for that uncertainty to be stated plainly instead of treating an estimate as a record.

Ask what the bird is accustomed to eating, how it responds to unfamiliar people and what kinds of interaction it currently accepts. A broad species description cannot tell you whether one individual welcomes hands, prefers a perch or needs extra time to settle. Find out what observations can be shared before arranging a visit or making a decision.

Availability, rearing and experience

Crownwing welcomes enquiries about this group; ask directly which, if any, individual birds are available to discuss now. Stock and timing can change, and an enquiry is not confirmation of a particular bird. If you are asking about hand-rearing, ask what is known about that bird's rearing and weaning history. No rearing method or outcome should be assumed from a category page.

Invite an honest account of the bird's familiar foods, handling preferences, vocal habits and any transitions it has experienced. Ask how the bird is being supported to eat independently and what routine it is used to, without expecting a promise that it will quickly bond, talk or adapt. A clear handover of known facts helps you prepare a less disruptive first few weeks.

Costs, preparation and handover

Ask for the current price of the specific bird and an itemised explanation of anything included; do not infer either from a general listing. Budget beyond the initial purchase for appropriate housing, safe enrichment, food, routine care and contingency costs over a potentially decades-long commitment. Confirm any payment, reservation or collection arrangements directly before relying on them.

Discuss the practical handover: what food the bird is eating, what equipment it knows, what information will accompany it and how a collection date is agreed. Check that everyone at home is ready, that the enclosure and safe exercise area are prepared, and that a suitable caregiver is identified for absences. Take time to consider the answers rather than buying on impulse.

Choose for compatibility, not reputation

A Grey's reputation for intelligence or speech is not a measure of its suitability for a particular household. Explain your experience, daily schedule, noise tolerance and plans for children or other pets, then ask which known traits of the individual may be relevant. A responsible conversation should leave room for you to decide that the timing or match is not right.

If you visit, observe how the bird responds in its familiar setting and ask how introductions and transport will be handled. Avoid selecting solely for a dramatic phrase, immediate step-up or close contact in one meeting. The useful outcome is an informed picture of this bird's identity, routines and needs, with unanswered questions clearly distinguished from confirmed information.

Can an African Grey share a home with another parrot?

Possibly, but companionship between people does not predict compatibility between birds. Plan controlled introductions, separate feeding and resting resources, and enough room to keep them apart if either bird is uncomfortable.

How should I compare a Congo and a Timneh beyond appearance?

Confirm which type you are discussing, then compare that bird's actual routine, confidence and accepted interactions. Both need substantial mental activity and long-term planning, while size and individual preferences can differ.
